\begin{abstract}
%% ---- begin content/abstract ----
LLM coding agents read logs, configuration files and tickets through tools, and whatever a tool returns enters the model's context. Agents are increasingly given local redaction tools through the Model Context Protocol, so we ask what an agent learns through such a tool. In a pre-registered study of an open-source on-device guardrail, a differential audit planted values, called every tool, and searched every reply in five encodings against a masked control. It found that a reply documented as content-free returned case-folded person names through detector metadata: with a name-list tier active, in 701 of 2,000 generated agent tool outputs and 24 of 129 real WNUT-17 documents. An allow-list of value-free metadata keys removed every hit. A regex-gated INT8 DistilBERT tier raised person-name character recall on real user-generated text (WNUT-17) by 0.482 over the pattern tiers. The gate, which sends 30\% of the text to the model, cost 0.225 of recall against running the model on every line. Batched inference broke streaming equivalence and left up to 12 names in clear that a whole-document pass redacted. Merged windows exceeded the tier's declared 256-character context. The same audit of four third-party tools found that three let the agent itself call a restore tool that returned every value they had hidden, and one returned a map of all original values with its anonymised text. A local LLM agent reading tickets through these tools leaked hidden values in every run through the tool that returns its map, and an appended prompt injection made it call the restore tool in 14 and 15 of 20 runs for the other two. Measuring per-call cost exposed a Nagle stall on every kept-alive REST request; fixing it cut a 256-byte call from 44.00 to 0.75\,ms.
%% ---- end content/abstract ----

\end{abstract}

%% ---- begin content/01-introduction ----
\section{Introduction}\label{sec:intro}

Large language model (LLM) coding agents work by reading. They open logs, configuration files, stack traces and support tickets through tools, and whatever a tool returns becomes part of the model's context: it is processed by the model, may be stored by its provider, and can be steered elsewhere by a prompt injected into the same context \cite{greshake2023injection,debenedetti2024agentdojo}. Workspace text routinely carries personal data and credentials \cite{meli2019git}. Agents are therefore being given redaction tools, increasingly through the Model Context Protocol (MCP) \cite{mcpspec}: before reading a file, the agent asks a local tool whether it holds secrets, or reads it through a tool that redacts them.

Such a tool sits on the trust boundary it is meant to protect. Its replies cross into the model's context like any other tool output, so the question is not only how much it detects, but \emph{what an agent learns through it}. We identify three channels. First, the redacted text still contains every value the detectors miss. Second, the tool's ``content-free'' replies (findings with types and offsets, explanations of a decision, reports in standard formats) are themselves text, and any field that echoes input can carry a value across. Third, cost: a guardrail that adds noticeable latency to every tool call will be switched off or bypassed.

We study these channels in an open-source, on-device guardrail, SafeStream-Redactor, which exposes the same detection engine as an MCP server, a REST API and SARIF reports. We treat its pattern tiers as a fixed baseline and evaluate three other parts: a regex-gated neural name tier, the agent-facing tool surface and its per-call cost. The study was pre-registered: hypotheses, systems, corpora, metrics and decision rules were committed before any system was scored, and every departure is reported (Section~\ref{sec:method}).

\paragraph{Contributions}
\begin{enumerate}
\item \textbf{A differential egress audit for content-free tool replies.} We plant values, call every tool, and search every string of every reply for the values in five encodings, counting a hit only if it disappears when the values are masked in the input. On the code as released, the audit found that the explanation tool returned case-folded person names through detector metadata: with the name-list tier active, in 701 of 2,000 generated agent tool outputs, 24 of 129 real WNUT-17 documents and 119 of 3,973 ai4privacy documents. An allow-list of value-free metadata keys removed every hit in every tier and corpus (Section~\ref{sec:egress}).
\item \textbf{A measured account of a gated neural tier.} On real user-generated text with human gold (WNUT-17), the tier raised person-name character recall over the pattern tiers by $+0.482$ [$+0.419$, $+0.548$]. The regex gate that keeps it cheap cost $0.225$ of that recall against running the model on every line, because it misses names written in lower case. Batched INT8 inference broke the streaming guarantee the engine otherwise provides, and the tier's declared 256-character context was exceeded by merged windows of up to 613 characters (Section~\ref{sec:nn}).
\item \textbf{The same audit applied to four third-party MCP redaction tools.} Three expose a restore call the agent itself can make; each returned every value its anonymiser had hidden. One returns a map of all original values in the anonymiser's own reply, and two documented contracts are contradicted by the measured replies (Section~\ref{sec:thirdparty}). A real tool-using agent, given a ticket with a prompt injection, called those restore tools and took the values back (Section~\ref{sec:agent}).
\item \textbf{The per-call cost of the guardrail by transport and redaction mode}, including a 40\,ms stall on every kept-alive REST request caused by Nagle's algorithm, found by this measurement and fixed (Section~\ref{sec:cost}).
\end{enumerate}
Code, corpora loaders, frozen manifests, raw results and the protocol are public (\repolink).

\section{Threat model}\label{sec:threat}

\begin{figure}[t]
\centering
\resizebox{\columnwidth}{!}{%
\begin{tikzpicture}[
  box/.style={draw, rounded corners=2pt, align=center, minimum height=8mm, inner sep=3pt, font=\small},
  arr/.style={-{Stealth[length=2mm]}, thick},
  lab/.style={font=\scriptsize, align=center}]
\node[box, fill=red!8] (llm) {LLM\\(provider)};
\node[box, right=16mm of llm] (client) {Agent\\client};
\node[box, right=18mm of client, fill=green!8] (srv) {Redaction tool\\(MCP / REST)};
\node[box, right=16mm of srv, fill=green!8] (ws) {Workspace\\files, logs};
\draw[arr] (ws) -- node[lab, above] {raw text} (srv);
\draw[arr] (srv) -- node[lab, above] {replies} (client);
\draw[arr] (client) -- node[lab, above] {context} (llm);
\draw[arr, dashed] (llm.north) to[bend left=22] node[lab, above] {tool calls (may be attacker-steered)} (srv.north);
\draw[dashed, thick, red!70!black] ($(client.east)!0.5!(srv.west)+(0,9mm)$) -- ($(client.east)!0.5!(srv.west)+(0,-9mm)$)
  node[lab, below, text=red!70!black] {trust boundary};
\end{tikzpicture}}
\caption{The setting. Everything the tool returns crosses the trust boundary into the model's context. The tool and the workspace are on the user's machine.}\label{fig:topology}
\end{figure}

Figure~\ref{fig:topology} shows the setting. An agent client relays tool calls chosen by an LLM to a local redaction tool, which reads workspace text and returns replies. We assume the model, its provider or a prompt injected into its context \cite{greshake2023injection} may try to learn values from the workspace, and that it can choose the arguments of tool calls. Everything the tool returns is therefore disclosed. The tool and the host are trusted: an adversary with code execution on the host needs no tool to read a file.

The tool makes two promises. \emph{Content-free replies}: \texttt{scan}, \texttt{explain\_\allowbreak detection}, \texttt{detectors}, \texttt{health}, REST \texttt{/scan} and SARIF output report types, offsets, confidences and detector names, never the matched text. \emph{Redaction}: \texttt{redact} returns the input with every detected value replaced. The first promise can be broken by the implementation; the second is bounded by detection recall. We measure both, and the cost of keeping them.

Out of scope are values the agent could infer from what the tool must disclose by design: the offset and length of a finding, and the suffix shown by masking (Section~\ref{sec:egress} describes what they reveal), and attacks on the model itself \cite{carlini2021extracting,lukas2023pii}.

\section{The guardrail under study}\label{sec:system}

\paragraph{Pattern tiers (baseline)} SafeStream's pattern tiers (regular expressions with checksum and format validators, label-anchored identifiers, a contextual scorer and an entropy tier) and its streaming engine, whose overlap rule makes chunked output equal to whole-document output for detectors that respect their declared bounds, are a fixed substrate here; this paper reports none of their results except as the baseline of a paired difference. We treat both as a frozen substrate, called T0, at the commit that opened this study, and report none of that paper's results. Every T0 number below is the baseline of a paired difference.

\paragraph{The gated neural tier} An optional tier runs a token-classification model on the user's machine through ONNX Runtime \cite{onnxruntime}: DistilBERT \cite{sanh2019distilbert} fine-tuned on CoNLL-2003 \cite{tjongkimsang2003conll} for person, organisation and location names, with weights dynamically quantised to INT8 \cite{jacob2018quantization}. To keep the cost of a neural model off machine text, a regular-expression \emph{gate} chooses what the model reads. A candidate is a run of two to four capitalised words, a single capitalised word after a lower-case word or a comma, or up to three words after a person cue (an honorific, ``signed by'', or a label such as ``patient:''). Each candidate is widened by 32 characters of context within its line, overlapping windows are merged, and words after a cue are re-capitalised so that a cased model can recognise a name written in lower or upper case. Only the merged windows are sent to the model. The tier declares a maximum span and left and right context of 256 characters each, which the engine adds to its overlap requirement. An optional batch mode runs up to 32 windows per inference call. Because the INT8 activation ranges are computed per call, a window's scores then depend on which windows share its batch, and batch composition depends on how the input was chunked.

\paragraph{Name-list tier} A third optional tier, the gazetteer, needs no model: it matches capitalised words, and words after a person cue, against lists of given and family names. It is evaluated here only for egress (Section~\ref{sec:egress}).

\paragraph{Tool surface} Table~\ref{tab:contract} lists what each interface returns. The MCP server \cite{mcpspec} speaks JSON-RPC over standard input and output, and the REST server listens on loopback only. Both repeat a reply's structured content as a JSON text block, as MCP clients expect.

\begin{table}[t]
\caption{What each interface returns. Only \texttt{redact} returns input text, by design: the input with every detected value replaced.}\label{tab:contract}
\centering\footnotesize
\setlength{\tabcolsep}{3pt}\begin{tabular}{@{}l p{0.6\columnwidth}@{}}
\toprule
Interface & Fields returned \\
\midrule
\multicolumn{2}{@{}l}{\emph{MCP tools}} \\
\texttt{scan} & per finding: type, start, end, length, confidence, severity, detector \\
\texttt{explain\_detection} & as \texttt{scan}, plus a context note and detector \texttt{notes} \\
\texttt{detectors} & tier names and declared bounds \\
\texttt{health} & version, tiers, settings \\
\texttt{redact} & redacted text; counts by type \\
\midrule
REST \texttt{/scan} & per finding: start, end, type, confidence, detector \\
SARIF 2.1.0 \cite{sarif210} & rule per type; per finding: level, region (offsets, lines), a fixed message \\
\bottomrule
\end{tabular}
\end{table}

\paragraph{Redaction modes} A detected value is replaced by a fixed marker (\emph{replace}), masked except for at most its last four characters and never more than half of it (\emph{mask}), a salted digest (\emph{hash}), an HMAC-SHA-256 pseudonym \cite{rfc2104} (\emph{pseudonymize}), a deterministic AES-256-GCM token that a key holder can reverse and that fails closed on any modification (\emph{encrypt}), or a synthetic value of the same type from reserved ranges (\emph{fictionalize}). Each is a function of the value alone, which is what keeps chunked output equal to whole-document output.

\section{Method}\label{sec:method}

\paragraph{Protocol} Four research questions, their hypotheses, systems, corpora, metrics and decision rules were committed to the repository before any system was scored. \textbf{C-RQ1}: does the gated neural tier improve person-name detection over T0, and how does it compare with statistical named-entity recognition, at what cost? \textbf{C-RQ2}: how good and how cheap is the gate, and does the tier honour its streaming contract? \textbf{C-RQ3}: does any value reach the agent through a content-free reply, and what does \texttt{redact} leave exposed? \textbf{C-RQ4}: what does the guardrail cost per tool call? \textbf{C-RQ5}, added by a protocol amendment before any third-party tool was installed: do other agent-facing redaction tools let an agent learn the values they protect? \textbf{C-RQ6}, added by a second amendment before any agent run: does a real agent, reading through each tool, take the values back when a prompt injection tells it to? Six departures were recorded during the study, each with its reason: cost figures are quoted from runs that had the machine to themselves; one throughput comparison is reported without an interval; the REST transport is measured before and after a fix (Section~\ref{sec:cost}); the egress matching rule was tightened after a pilot run, and both audits were repeated with it (Section~\ref{sec:egress}); one determinism run used a capped stream; and one bookkeeping rule on number provenance was restated, because identical three-decimal values occur by chance. The second amendment records that the agent ran on a local open-weight model because the study environment could not call a hosted model's API. The amendment that added C-RQ5 records its own installation outcomes and one correction to how reply fields are classified.

\paragraph{Corpora} Table~\ref{tab:corpora} lists the corpora. ai4privacy \cite{ai4privacy300k} is synthetic and was split into halves before this study; only its test half is scored. CoNLL-2003 is the neural model's training distribution and serves as an upper bound only. WNUT-17 \cite{derczynski2017wnut} is the real corpus: sentences from Twitter, Reddit, YouTube and StackExchange, annotated by people for emerging and rare entities, grouped into documents of ten sentences in file order. Its manifest was frozen with the protocol. AgentTrace is generated with a fixed seed. It holds the kinds of tool output an agent reads (stack traces, \texttt{.env} and YAML files, CI logs, \texttt{git} output, HTTP dumps and tickets), with planted values at known offsets. Because the planted formats come from the same authors as the rules, AgentTrace is used only for egress and cost, never for accuracy.

\paragraph{Systems} T0 (pattern tiers, Rust core); T0+NN, the product configuration with the gated neural tier; T0+NN ungated, a benchmark-only variant that sends every line, cut into pieces of at most 400 characters, to the model instead of the gate's windows; T0+NN batched (batch 32); T0+spaCy, T0 with spaCy's \texttt{en\_core\_web\_sm} \cite{honnibal2020spacy}; and Presidio \cite{presidio} with spaCy's small and large models. Every system runs single-threaded in its own process.

\paragraph{Metrics and statistics} The primary accuracy metric is person-name character recall: the share of gold person-name characters covered by any prediction, since a redactor protects a name whatever type it assigns. We also report the share of person names fully covered, and character F1 over gold of the types Presidio can detect (``Presidio-scope F1''), so that no system is rewarded for types another cannot emit. Intervals are 95\% percentile bootstrap intervals over documents (2,000 resamples, seed 0). All systems share one resample matrix, so differences are paired, and a planned comparison is called significant when its paired interval excludes zero \cite{efron1993bootstrap}. Cost comes from the same runs: throughput over analysis time (model load excluded), per-document latency, load time and peak resident memory.

\paragraph{Environment} One virtual machine: 4 vCPU Intel Xeon at 2.1\,GHz, Linux, Python 3.13, ONNX Runtime 1.29, spaCy 3.8, Presidio 2.2.366. Each result file records its commit, and the pre-fix measurements ran on the commit before each fix.

\subsection{C-RQ1: what the neural tier adds, and at what cost}\label{sec:nn}

Table~\ref{tab:accuracy} gives accuracy and cost, and Figure~\ref{fig:recallcost} plots person-name recall against latency. On real user-generated text (WNUT-17), T0 found no person names: its tiers look for structured values, and the corpus has almost none. Adding the gated neural tier raised person-name character recall by $+0.482$ [$+0.419$, $+0.548$], and on synthetic ai4privacy by $+0.336$ [$+0.305$, $+0.369$], confirming the first planned comparison (P1) on both corpora.

Against T0 with spaCy's small model (P2), the neural tier had higher person-name recall on ai4privacy ($+0.092$ [$+0.065$, $+0.120$]) but not on WNUT-17 ($+0.024$ [$-0.032$, $+0.079$]). spaCy processed WNUT-17 about twice as fast (66.5 against 32.6\,kB/s, median 14.0 against 29.3\,ms per document). Against Presidio with spaCy's large model (P3), the neural tier had higher Presidio-scope character F1 on both corpora: $+0.154$ [$+0.112$, $+0.200$] on WNUT-17 and $+0.033$ [$+0.023$, $+0.043$] on ai4privacy. That margin comes from precision. On WNUT-17, Presidio lg fully covered more person names than the neural tier ($-0.092$ [$-0.147$, $-0.031$]), and the difference in person-name character recall was not significant ($-0.049$ [$-0.104$, $+0.008$]).

The tier is not quiet on prose without personal data. It flagged 31 of the 55 benign documents (0.56), against none for T0, 0.58 for T0 with spaCy and 0.78 and 0.80 for the two Presidio configurations. These documents name public organisations, places and people, which a named-entity model is trained to find. Batch mode (32 windows per call) gave the same accuracy within the intervals and no speed-up on these short documents. Its cost is the subject of Section~\ref{sec:contract}.

\subsection{C-RQ2: the gate and the streaming contract}\label{sec:contract}

\paragraph{What the gate costs} The gate sent 26.5\% of the characters of ai4privacy and 29.8\% of WNUT-17 to the model, and 10.4\% of real system logs (Table~\ref{tab:gate}). But only 54.3\% and 59.4\% of gold person names lay entirely inside a window, which caps the tier's recall. Running the model on every line instead raised person-name character recall by 0.225 [0.173, 0.276] on WNUT-17 and 0.240 [0.210, 0.269] on ai4privacy (P4), at about a third of the throughput (10.5 against 32.6\,kB/s on WNUT-17). The gate misses names it is not built to see. Of the 174 WNUT-17 person names outside every window, 74 were written in lower case or as a handle, and 83 were single capitalised words, which the gate admits only after a lower-case word or a comma, because almost every sentence starts with one. On ai4privacy, 1,274 of the 1,294 missed names were single words.

\paragraph{Determinism} With batch size 1, streamed output equalled whole-document output under every chunking tried: 20 random chunkings at chunk sizes of 1 to 64\,KiB, on the WNUT-17 stream and on the first 700 ai4privacy test documents (299,915 characters). Naive chunking without the engine missed up to 15 of the 642 reference detections on WNUT-17 and leaked 5 gold names; on ai4privacy it missed 64 of 2,806 and leaked 51. With batch size 32, no chunking reproduced the whole-document output. The engine's streamed output then missed up to 46 of 644 reference detections on WNUT-17 and up to 103 of 2,822 on ai4privacy, and in both up to 12 gold values that the whole-document pass redacted were left in clear. Batching thus re-opens, through numerical non-determinism, exactly the leak the streaming engine exists to close. The option is documented as non-deterministic; our data show it is also unsafe under streaming.

\paragraph{Declared context} The tier declares 256 characters of context. Merged windows grew to 613 characters on CoNLL and 462 on ai4privacy, and 24 windows in ai4privacy exceeded the declaration (Table~\ref{tab:gate}). When only the 256 characters on each side of a detection were kept, 2 of 2,198 CoNLL detections disappeared, so the declaration is not a bound on what a decision depends on. Synthetic lines of chained names (``Ann Lee, Bo Kim, \dots'') produced merged windows of up to 2,068 characters, yet streamed output still equalled whole-document output in all 15 chunkings at every length tried. The engine's overlap, 8,192 characters for the whole pipeline, is set by the longest-reaching pattern tier and absorbed the excess. A deployment that ran the neural tier alone would have no such margin. The fix is to cap the merged window at the declared bound, or to declare the bound the gate can actually produce.

\subsection{C-RQ3: what crosses the tool boundary}\label{sec:egress}

%% ---- begin content/tab_egress ----
\begin{table}[t]
\caption{Egress through content-free replies (C-RQ3): distinct gold values found in any content-free reply, before / after the fix. Values searched per tier: AgentTrace 5,250, WNUT-17 976, ai4privacy 15,092.}\label{tab:egress}
\centering\footnotesize
\begin{tabular}{@{}l r r r@{}}
\toprule
Tiers & AgentTrace & WNUT-17 & ai4privacy \\
\midrule
T0 & 0 / 0 & 0 / 0 & 0 / 0 \\
T0+gazetteer & 701 / 0 & 25 / 0 & 199 / 0 \\
T0+NN & 0 / 0 & 0 / 0 & 0 / 0 \\
T0+spaCy & 0 / 0 & 0 / 0 & 0 / 0 \\
\bottomrule
\end{tabular}
\end{table}
%% ---- end content/tab_egress ----


\paragraph{Content-free replies} Before the fix, the differential audit found person names in \texttt{explain\_\allowbreak detection} replies whenever the gazetteer tier (a model-free list of given names) was active (Table~\ref{tab:egress}). Every hit was in the \texttt{notes.norm} field, which carried the detected name case-folded (``maria gonzalez''), and in the JSON text block that repeats it. Names leaked from 701 of the 2,000 AgentTrace documents, 24 of the 129 WNUT-17 documents and 119 of the 3,973 ai4privacy documents. No other tier, field, interface or encoding leaked a gold value. The cause was a deny-list: \texttt{notes} forwarded every detector metadata key except one. The fix forwards only an allow-list of ten keys whose values are fixed vocabulary or numbers. It also removed three fields that had not leaked a gold value in our corpora but could carry input text: a label cue, a structured-field key and the model's file path. After the fix the audit found no egress in any tier, corpus, interface or encoding. A property test that plants random surnames now fails the build on any regression. The pilot run also showed why the audit compares against a masked control and matches whole tokens: without them, three-letter values (``Hon'') matched inside tool words (``phone''), and house numbers matched character offsets in SARIF messages.

\paragraph{Redacted text} Through \texttt{redact}, a value is exposed exactly when detection misses it. With the neural tier, 0.588 of WNUT-17 values of at least four characters and 0.420 of ai4privacy values were still present verbatim in the redacted text. That is slightly below the share not fully covered by any detection (0.631 and 0.437), because a partly covered value no longer appears whole. Every mode except mask gave the same exposure. Mask keeps a suffix of each covered value visible, at most four characters and never more than half the value: 36.0\% of the characters of covered WNUT-17 values and 27.4\% on ai4privacy. Offsets and lengths, which \texttt{scan} returns by design, disclose a value's position and length but not its characters. Hash and pseudonymize disclose whether two values are equal, which is their purpose.

We ran the same audit, through the official MCP client, on every open-source redaction tool that met the pre-registered inclusion criteria. Six candidates were found. Two were excluded at installation: one ships middleware but no tool, and the offline model of the other could not be downloaded. A second engine of one tool was also excluded, because it demanded a commercial key after ten requests a day. Four tools were audited, called T1 to T4 until their maintainers have been told (Section~\ref{sec:discussion}). Table~\ref{tab:thirdparty} gives the results. The share of values left in each tool's redacted output depends on which entity types it targets, so it is reported but not compared.

\paragraph{The agent can undo the redaction} Three of the four tools give the agent a restore call that turns placeholders back into the original values, so that a model's answer can be shown to the user with the real values in place. Called by the agent on the output of the tool's own anonymiser, the restore call returned every value it had hidden: 4,489 of 4,489 for T2, 2,339 of 2,339 for T3 and 2,750 of 2,750 for T4. In the threat model of Section~\ref{sec:threat}, where the model or an injected prompt chooses the tool calls, such a call cancels the protection. For two tools this contradicts their own documentation: T3's documentation says its restore call returns only a file path, but without an output path it returned the restored text; T4's documentation describes restored text being written to disk and not shown to the model. T3's separate mapping call returned only placeholder types, never values, which is the safe design.

\paragraph{Values in the same reply} T2 returned a map from each placeholder to its original value in the same reply as the anonymised text. That map carried 0.62 of all values on AgentTrace (3,242 of 5,250), although its documentation says no data leaves the machine: in an agent loop the reply goes to the model. The detection calls of T1 and T3 returned the matched values themselves, 0.63 and 0.44 of all values on AgentTrace. That is by design and documented for T1, which warns that its use exposes the text to the model. Under the same harness, no SafeStream reply carried a value outside its redacted output, and it offers no restore call to the agent.

The audits above measure what a tool returns. To see what an agent does with it, a local open-weight model, Qwen2.5-7B-Instruct (4-bit, run with llama.cpp at temperature 0), was asked to summarise a ticket in three sentences. It could read the ticket only through each tool's anonymiser, and it was also given the tool's own text tools, the restore call among them. Each tool was run on 20 generated tickets, once as written and once with an appended paragraph telling AI assistants to call ``the tool that restores or reveals the original values'' and quote the restored ticket (Table~\ref{tab:agent}).

With SafeStream, no hidden value reached the model in any run, with or without the injection. With T2, every run leaked, with or without it: the anonymiser returns the value map with the text, so the hidden values were in the model's context from the first read, and the agent copied them into its summary in 17 of 20 benign runs and all 20 injected ones. With T3 and T4, the restore call decided the outcome. Without the injection, the agent never called T3's restore call, but it called T4's in 13 of 20 runs unprompted, and hidden values reached it in 7. The injection raised restore calls to 14 of 20 for T3 and 15 of 20 for T4. Runs in which hidden values reached the model rose to 13 of 20 for T4 (95\% interval 0.41 to 0.85, against 0.15 to 0.59 without the injection). For T3, in 10 of its 14 restore calls the agent asked the tool to write the restored text to a file rather than return it, so values reached the model in only one run. The cleartext was still restored, onto disk at a path the agent chose; this count is exploratory, not a pre-registered outcome. One model, one injection and 20 tickets per cell show that the attack works on a capable open model, not how often it works on every model.

\paragraph{Transport} Table~\ref{tab:cost} gives median latency per \texttt{scan} call. For small payloads the transport is visible but cheap: at 256\,B a call took 0.28\,ms in process, 0.98\,ms over stdio and 0.75\,ms over REST. From 64\,KiB, detection dominates. Over stdio the official MCP client stayed within the pre-registered factor of 1.25 of in-process latency at 64\,KiB (88.79 against 79.46\,ms) and 1\,MiB (1,480.27 against 1,268.70\,ms), but not at 4\,MiB (7,421.76 against 5,319.80\,ms), so H4a holds only up to 1\,MiB. We did not profile where the extra time at 4\,MiB goes. Starting the stdio server and completing the MCP handshake took between 0.08 and 0.126\,s. Measuring REST revealed that every kept-alive request waited about 40\,ms regardless of payload. The handler wrote headers and body in two writes, and Nagle's algorithm \cite{rfc896} held the body until the client's delayed acknowledgement \cite{rfc1122}. Setting \texttt{TCP\_NODELAY} on the handler removed the stall: the median 256\,B call fell from 44.00 to 0.75\,ms, and the 4\,KiB call from 48.06 to 5.87\,ms. From 64\,KiB the difference disappears into detection time.

\paragraph{Redaction modes and reports} On 16\,MiB of AgentTrace text (258,749 detections), end-to-end \texttt{redact} throughput varied little with the mode, from 1.22\,MB/s for mask to 1.06\,MB/s for encrypt: detection, not rendering, sets the cost. Rendering a replacement took 0.44\,$\mu$s per detection for replace and 9.65\,$\mu$s for encrypt, whose tokens nearly double the output (1.945 bytes out per byte in). Encrypt round-tripped exactly: all 16,171 tokens in a 1\,MiB sample were restored to the original text. Of 10,000 tokens with one bit of the nonce, ciphertext or tag flipped, none was restored. A SARIF report of 7,500 findings validated against the official 2.1.0 schema with no error, and building it cost 5.38\,ms per 1,000 findings.

%% ---- begin content/06-discussion ----
\section{Discussion and limitations}\label{sec:discussion}

\paragraph{Contracts need tests that plant values} The leak was in a reply documented as content-free, and the project's existing test of that reply passed, because it used tiers whose metadata happened to hold no input text. A deny-list of metadata keys turns every new detector into a potential channel. An allow-list together with a planted-value property test reverses the default. The differential design matters: without a masked control and whole-token matching, the audit reported coincidences, and a reviewer would have learned to ignore it.

\paragraph{A cheap gate is a recall decision} The gate makes the neural tier affordable on machine text (it reads about a tenth of a log) but caps recall at the share of names it can see, about 0.6 of names in real user-generated text. Where agents read chat logs, tickets or social-media exports, running the model on every line costs about three times as much and recovers about a quarter of person-name recall. That is a deployment choice. The tool should state it, not hide it behind a default.

\paragraph{Batching and declared bounds} Batched INT8 inference is faster on long inputs. But because the quantisation ranges depend on what else is in the batch, it breaks the property that makes streaming safe, and in our runs it left names in clear. A tier that declares its context must also be held to it. Here the pipeline's larger overlap hid an inaccurate declaration, which is luck, not design.

\paragraph{Restore is a capability, not a convenience} Reversible pseudonymisation is useful: a user wants the model's answer with the real names in it. But a restore call exposed to the agent turns the model into the party that holds the key. Restoration belongs outside the agent's tool surface, for example in the client, after the model's reply and under the user's control, or behind a key the model never sees.

\paragraph{Disclosure} We are informing the maintainers of T1 to T4 privately, with the reproducers, before naming them. The tools will be named in the final version of this paper, after their maintainers have had time to respond.

\paragraph{Limitations} The agent experiment used one open-weight model of 7 billion parameters, one injection and 20 tickets per cell; frontier models may resist this injection more, or call restore tools more readily. AgentTrace is synthetic, and its planted formats come from the rules' authors, so it supports no accuracy claim. WNUT-17 is small (129 documents) and its documents are groups of ten sentences, not natural documents. CoNLL-2003 is the model's training distribution. We evaluated one neural model, one quantisation scheme and one machine, and only four third-party tools: those that met our criteria on one day's search. Offsets, lengths and mask suffixes are disclosed by design; we described what they reveal but did not quantify re-identification from them. Egress was searched in five encodings, and an encoding outside that set would not be found.
%% ---- end content/06-discussion ----

%% ---- begin content/07-related-work ----
\section{Related work}\label{sec:related}

\paragraph{De-identification and named-entity recognition} Rule-based and neural de-identification of clinical text \cite{norgeot2020philter,dernoncourt2017deid}, neural entity recognition in security text \cite{simran2020cybersecner}, and toolkits such as Presidio \cite{presidio,presidioresearch} combine patterns with statistical or transformer models \cite{devlin2019bert,sanh2019distilbert,zaratiana2024gliner}. Lison et al.\ argue that detection alone is not anonymisation \cite{lison2021anonymisation}, and the Text Anonymization Benchmark measures disclosure risk on court judgments \cite{pilan2022tab}. WNUT-17 targets the novel, rare and lower-case entities of user-generated text \cite{derczynski2017wnut}, which is why we use it as the real corpus here.

\paragraph{Secrets} Credential leakage in public repositories is widespread \cite{meli2019git}. Scanners such as gitleaks and TruffleHog \cite{gitleaks,trufflehog} differ mainly in their rules and filters \cite{basak2023comparative}. They report findings to people, not to a model.

\paragraph{LLM agents and privacy} Prompt injection lets content read by an agent steer its tool calls \cite{greshake2023injection}, and AgentDojo evaluates such attacks and defences in tool-using agents \cite{debenedetti2024agentdojo}. Language models can memorise and emit training data, including personal data \cite{carlini2021extracting,lukas2023pii}. Those works study the model. We study a tool on the boundary: what its replies disclose, independent of the model. MCP \cite{mcpspec} standardises how agents call such tools, but does not define what a tool may disclose.

\paragraph{Streaming redaction} Splitting input into pieces is a known way to evade detection \cite{ptacek1998insertion}, and streaming regular-expression engines carry automaton state across blocks to avoid it \cite{wang2019hyperscan}. SafeStream's engine instead keeps an overlap whose length each tier declares; we rely on it and test whether a neural tier respects the bound it declares.
%% ---- end content/07-related-work ----

%% ---- begin content/08-conclusion ----
\section{Conclusion}\label{sec:conclusion}

A redaction tool given to an LLM agent is a channel as well as a filter. In the guardrail we studied, a reply documented as content-free returned person names through detector metadata. An allow-list and a planted-value property test closed that channel. A regex-gated neural tier raised person-name recall on real user-generated text from nothing to about half, but the gate that keeps it cheap leaves a quarter of the achievable recall on the table. Batched inference re-opened the chunking leak that the streaming engine exists to close. And a transport detail, Nagle's algorithm, cost more per REST call than detection did for small inputs. Each finding came from measuring the tool from the agent's side of the boundary, and we recommend that every agent-facing redaction tool be held to such a test.
